title: Sun's Surface Has Whirlpools That Could Spark Solar Flares
summary: Have you ever seen a whirlpool in a bathtub or a swimming pool? Now imagine one on the sun! The world's biggest solar telescope just took the most detailed pictures of the sun's surface ever. And guess what? It found giant swirls of superhot, charged gas called plasma. The sun is a giant ball of this plasma. These whirlpools might be the reason the sun sometimes throws out huge bursts of energy called solar flares. Solar flares are like giant explosions of light and radiation. They can mess with satellites, GPS, and even power grids on Earth. Scientists used the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Hawaii to take these pictures. It has a mirror 4 meters (13 feet) wide — that's about as long as a car! The telescope captured swirls across a patch of sun about 19 kilometers (12 miles) wide. That's wider than a big city. The swirls are caused by something called the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. That's a fancy way of saying: when two layers of fluid move at different speeds, they curl up into waves. You can see the same thing in ocean waves or clouds on Earth. Scientists have seen this on Jupiter and in the sun's atmosphere, but never on the sun's surface until now. This discovery could help us predict when solar flares will happen. That's important because those flares can affect technology we use every day.
why_it_matters: The same solar flares scientists want to predict can knock out GPS on your family's phone or the power in your town, so learning how the sun works helps keep everyday technology running.

background_read: The Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (the world's most powerful telescope built just for watching the sun, named after a U.S. senator from Hawaii) sits on a tall volcano in Hawaii so the sky above it stays clear.
When the sun throws out a big burst of energy, it can make colorful lights called auroras appear near Earth's poles, and strong bursts can bother satellites and radios.
The sun's activity rises and falls in a cycle that lasts about eleven years, so scientists keep watching with space missions like NASA's (the U.S. space agency) sun-watching spacecraft.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists using the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Hawaii.
WHAT: They took the most detailed pictures of the sun's surface ever and found giant whirlpools of plasma that may cause solar flares.
WHERE: On the sun's surface, seen by a telescope in Hawaii; the swirls covered a patch about 19 kilometers (12 miles) wide.
WHY: The discovery could help scientists predict solar flares, which can mess with satellites, GPS and power grids on Earth.

perspectives.description: Researchers are thrilled because these swirls have never been seen on the sun's surface before, and they give a new clue about how the sun works.
People who depend on satellites, GPS and electricity may worry, because big solar flares can damage or disrupt all of those systems.
Kids and stargazers may feel inspired, because the same curling wave pattern shows up in bathtubs, ocean waves and on Jupiter — science links things we see all the time.
